To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the auditory evoked potentials recorded from the scalp of the cat are generated by the brainstem auditory system, and that they can be detected by means of averaging at considerable distances from their generators.

In the cat, the scalp and rostral brain potentials evoked by a click, when averaged, show four positive waves (P1, P2, P3, P4) which are likely to represent the activity of the cochlear nucleus (P2), the superior olive (P3) and the inferior colliculi (P4).

(1) Volume-conducted potentials in the brainstem auditory pathway can be detected with a single electrode outside that pathway, (2) The potentials are detected by averaging, time- locked to the auditory click, and (3) The potentials are generated in and near classical auditory structures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of the location of the generators of the evoked potentials recorded from the scalp.
the use of the auditory evoked response (AER) in the cat to determine the site and extent of damage in the auditory system after acoustic trauma.
the problem of the origin of the auditory evoked potential (EP) recorded from the scalp of man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the technique of averaging has been shown to be of considerable value in the analysis of the responses of a sensory system to a single stimulus.
the volume-conducted potential recorded from the cat scalp is a composite of potentials generated in the VIIIth nerve, the cochlear nucleus and the inferior colliculi.

the auditory evoked potential recorded from the scalp in the cat, by means of the tongue reference, consists of four waves, P 1, N 1, P2 and P 4, with P 2, and P 3, and P 4 showing increased amplitude or inversion or both, in the vicinity of known auditory structures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the auditory evoked potentials recorded by averaging from the scalp of the anesthetized animal can be used to map the auditory system in the same way as the electrical responses of the visual system can be used to locate visual centers.
the volume-conducted potential is a useful tool for studying sensory systems.

the volume-conducted potentials in the cat auditory system are not a simple series of discrete events, each generated at a single location and each with a single polarity, but rather that each potential wave is a composite of several components, each of which may have a different generator and different polarity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the auditory cortex is not necessary for auditory perception, and the auditory cortex is a very small area.
the auditory brainstem response can be used to detect the presence and severity of hearing loss in infants.
it is possible to record from the brainstem using surface electrodes.
